1	---
2	name: drafts-inbox
3	description: Triage everything in the Drafts inbox — your always-available assistant inbox. Read each item, take action, and archive when done so the inbox stays the unprocessed queue.
4	triggers:
5	  - check my Drafts inbox
6	  - process my inbox
7	  - what's in Drafts
8	  - triage my Drafts inbox
9	  - drafts inbox triage
10	---
11	
12	# Drafts Inbox
13	
14	Triage the items sitting in the Drafts **inbox** — your capture-to-action pipeline. Archiving each item when it's handled means the inbox itself is the "unprocessed since last run" queue; there's no separate timestamp to track.
15	
16	## When to Use
17	
18	Use this skill at the start of a session or whenever you want to process items you've captured throughout the day via Drafts on iPhone, Apple Watch, or Mac.
19	
20	## Prerequisites
21	
22	- Drafts MCP connector must be set up.
23	
24	## Instructions
25	
26	1. Read the inbox with `drafts_get_drafts` (`folder: "inbox"`). This returns summaries only (title, dates, flags, tags), not full content.
27	2. **Check the volume first.** If the inbox is large (more than ~20 items, i.e. a backlog rather than a session's worth), don't try to process everything blindly. Report the count and date range, and ask how far back to go (e.g. this month, last 3 months, flagged only, or the whole backlog). Default to the most recent window.
28	   - The MCP returns the full inbox; use the `modificationDate` field to filter to the chosen window yourself. `drafts_get_drafts` also accepts `modifiedAfter` / `flagged` to narrow the pull.
29	3. Present a numbered list of the in-scope items with a brief preview of each.
30	4. For each item, pull its full content with `drafts_get_draft` (the summary title is truncated), classify it, and take the appropriate action:
31	
32	| Type | Action |
33	|------|--------|
34	| **Task or to-do** | Capture to OmniFocus via `omnifocus-capture` (inbox by default). Flag if urgent. |
35	| **Writing idea (substantial)** | Create a Writing Task in `APR/TaskNotes/Tasks/` (frontmatter: `status`, `priority`, `dateCreated`/`dateModified`, `tags: [task]`, `ContentType: Blog`/`Newsletter`/`Glossary`). |
36	| **Content hook (one-liner)** | Add to the running `APR/Efforts/Content Ideas.md` note. |
37	| **Research request** | Do the research and report findings. |
38	| **Quick instruction** | Execute the instruction (file a note, move a file, look something up). |
39	| **Question** | Answer the question. |
40	| **Reference / clipping** | File it where it belongs (vault note, DevonThink, etc.) or note that it's already captured elsewhere. |
41	| **Unclear** | Ask for clarification before acting. |
42	
43	5. After processing each item, archive the draft with `drafts_archive`.
44	6. Report what was done: "[N] items processed. [Brief summary of actions taken.]"
45	
46	## Rules
47	
48	- Process items one at a time. Don't batch everything silently. (For a large backlog, a grouped proposal with a per-item action is fine, but get approval before archiving or capturing anything.)
49	- When an item is ambiguous, ask rather than guess.
50	- Archive each draft only after it's been fully processed — the archive is what marks it "done," so never archive something you skipped.
51	- If an item requires a tool you don't have access to, note it and move on (leave it in the inbox).
52	- Confirm before deleting; default to archive, not trash.
53

---
name: drafts-inbox
description: Triage everything in the Drafts inbox — your always-available assistant inbox. Read each item, take action, and archive when done so the inbox stays the unprocessed queue.
triggers:
  - check my Drafts inbox
  - process my inbox
  - what's in Drafts
  - triage my Drafts inbox
  - drafts inbox triage
---

# Drafts Inbox

Triage the items sitting in the Drafts **inbox** — your capture-to-action pipeline. Archiving each item when it's handled means the inbox itself is the "unprocessed since last run" queue; there's no separate timestamp to track.

## When to Use

Use this skill at the start of a session or whenever you want to process items you've captured throughout the day via Drafts on iPhone, Apple Watch, or Mac.

## Prerequisites

- Drafts MCP connector must be set up.

## Instructions

1. Read the inbox with `drafts_get_drafts` (`folder: "inbox"`). This returns summaries only (title, dates, flags, tags), not full content.
2. **Check the volume first.** If the inbox is large (more than ~20 items, i.e. a backlog rather than a session's worth), don't try to process everything blindly. Report the count and date range, and ask how far back to go (e.g. this month, last 3 months, flagged only, or the whole backlog). Default to the most recent window.
   - The MCP returns the full inbox; use the `modificationDate` field to filter to the chosen window yourself. `drafts_get_drafts` also accepts `modifiedAfter` / `flagged` to narrow the pull.
3. Present a numbered list of the in-scope items with a brief preview of each.
4. For each item, pull its full content with `drafts_get_draft` (the summary title is truncated), classify it, and take the appropriate action:

| Type | Action |
|------|--------|
| **Task or to-do** | Capture to OmniFocus via `omnifocus-capture` (inbox by default). Flag if urgent. |
| **Writing idea (substantial)** | Create a Writing Task in `APR/TaskNotes/Tasks/` (frontmatter: `status`, `priority`, `dateCreated`/`dateModified`, `tags: [task]`, `ContentType: Blog`/`Newsletter`/`Glossary`). |
| **Content hook (one-liner)** | Add to the running `APR/Efforts/Content Ideas.md` note. |
| **Research request** | Do the research and report findings. |
| **Quick instruction** | Execute the instruction (file a note, move a file, look something up). |
| **Question** | Answer the question. |
| **Reference / clipping** | File it where it belongs (vault note, DevonThink, etc.) or note that it's already captured elsewhere. |
| **Unclear** | Ask for clarification before acting. |

5. After processing each item, archive the draft with `drafts_archive`.
6. Report what was done: "[N] items processed. [Brief summary of actions taken.]"

## Rules

- Process items one at a time. Don't batch everything silently. (For a large backlog, a grouped proposal with a per-item action is fine, but get approval before archiving or capturing anything.)
- When an item is ambiguous, ask rather than guess.
- Archive each draft only after it's been fully processed — the archive is what marks it "done," so never archive something you skipped.
- If an item requires a tool you don't have access to, note it and move on (leave it in the inbox).
- Confirm before deleting; default to archive, not trash.

---

*Started with the Robot Assistant Field Guide Starter Kit. Customized in Video 6 via the assembler. Updated 2026-06-28 to triage the whole inbox instead of a "cowork" tag.*

  "title": "One of my readers pointed out that no LLM can recommend a trustworthy bike shop. That's true. Luckily, I didn't need an LLM, I already had a good idea that Full Cycle would be a good choice. Especially since they're among the few bike shops that do bike fittings.",
  "content": "One of my readers pointed out that no LLM can recommend a trustworthy bike shop. That's true. Luckily, I didn't need an LLM, I already had a good idea that Full Cycle would be a good choice. Especially since they're among the few bike shops that do bike fittings.\n\nI went to the fitting expecting I'd buy either a Giant Revolt 0 or a Norco Search GRX. Both bikes around $C2500-2600 before tax and additional parts (pedals, pannier rack, cadence sensor.)\n\nIn the fitting process, we tried a Revolt 0 and then a Norco Search A Cues. As we were working, he asked more and more questions about my needs. In the end, he pointed out the Norco used cheaper, slightly heavier parts that'll actually last longer. Instead of getting fancier components, he said any modern gravel bike will be massively better than my nearly 20-year-old hybrid Trek. I asked about tubeless tires and a few other things, and he said the tires the bike comes with are very good.\n\nHis whole message, buy a cheaper bike. Ride for a couple of thousand kms, see what needs changing, and only then pay for something better.\n\nMy bike is ready for pickup, so it's time to play.",

content.text:
{
  "id": "48510391-7E82-4678-90E6-A018E135DDC0",
  "title": "Position on AI",
  "content": "Position on AI

I use it every day. I use it to work on my website and automate many small tasks that I wouldn't do otherwise. I even use it on some development-related work, effectively a BDD-type approach**. If you want a good source of ideas on how to use it day-to-day try David Sparks' [Robot Assistant Field Guide](https://learn.macsparky.com/p/rafg26).

I'm not arguing against using it. I'm arguing against the way most of the conversation around it is happening.

A few things I keep coming back to:
- **Hype outweighs reality** The gap between what is promised and what actually happens is large. The most recent example of this is the Mythos model from Anthropic. They promised it's finding new flaws in code. The reality from people who looked closely is that it's chaining together existing classes of flaws, with the aide of people who really understand security. Useful, yes. World-changing? No. We're sold a miracle and it's a lot more complicated.
- **The flaws are underplayed** I've started a working draft on this: [AI Failure Modes for Agile Teams](https://agilepainrelief.com/downloads/ai-failure-modes-for-agile-teams.pdf). It's early and intended for newsletter subscribers, so please don't share it further. (Feedback would be appreciated.)
- **Wrong place, wrong problem** Too many organisations are putting it where it damages the system around it (i.e. Generating code) instead of improving the system (Assisting in Discovery i.e. Lean Startup and Lean UX).

I've been writing about this for the past year: [AI posts on Agile Pain Relief](https://agilepainrelief.com/blog/category/artificial-intelligence/). And I've just released a course aimed at people who want a grounded, evidence-based way to think about it all: [Surviving the AI Tsunami](https://agilepainrelief.com/surviving-the-ai-tsunami-an-evidenced-based-course/).

What I find missing in most discussions is any serious look at the 2nd and 3rd order effects. Everyone is focused on "what can it do right now" and almost no one is asking "what does a system look like once enough of it is in place."

I'd like to find a few other people thinking along similar lines, so we can talk every few weeks and share what we're learning. If that's you, let me know. I'm also happy to share the reading list I've built up so far.

Draft captured from Drafts inbox (originally written 2026-05-30). Position/stance essay + a call to find others thinking about 2nd/3rd-order effects.

---

Position on AI

I use it every day. I use it to work on my website and automate many small tasks that I wouldn't do otherwise. I even use it on some development-related work, effectively a BDD-type approach**. If you want a good source of ideas on how to use it day-to-day try David Sparks' [Robot Assistant Field Guide](https://learn.macsparky.com/p/rafg26).

I'm not arguing against using it. I'm arguing against the way most of the conversation around it is happening.

A few things I keep coming back to:
- **Hype outweighs reality** The gap between what is promised and what actually happens is large. The most recent example of this is the Mythos model from Anthropic. They promised it's finding new flaws in code. The reality from people who looked closely is that it's chaining together existing classes of flaws, with the aide of people who really understand security. Useful, yes. World-changing? No. We're sold a miracle and it's a lot more complicated.
- **The flaws are underplayed** I've started a working draft on this: [AI Failure Modes for Agile Teams](https://agilepainrelief.com/downloads/ai-failure-modes-for-agile-teams.pdf). It's early and intended for newsletter subscribers, so please don't share it further. (Feedback would be appreciated.)
- **Wrong place, wrong problem** Too many organisations are putting it where it damages the system around it (i.e. Generating code) instead of improving the system (Assisting in Discovery i.e. Lean Startup and Lean UX).

I've been writing about this for the past year: [AI posts on Agile Pain Relief](https://agilepainrelief.com/blog/category/artificial-intelligence/). And I've just released a course aimed at people who want a grounded, evidence-based way to think about it all: [Surviving the AI Tsunami](https://agilepainrelief.com/surviving-the-ai-tsunami-an-evidenced-based-course/).

What I find missing in most discussions is any serious look at the 2nd and 3rd order effects. Everyone is focused on "what can it do right now" and almost no one is asking "what does a system look like once enough of it is in place."

I'd like to find a few other people thinking along similar lines, so we can talk every few weeks and share what we're learning. If that's you, let me know. I'm also happy to share the reading list I've built up so far.

  "id": "860BEADB-FDFF-4E57-9F41-796D9864A4D1",
  "title": "Reshuffle",
  "content": "Reshuffle

The music industry is a good example of the change that is being unleashed by AI.

Music came in albums and required a record company's backing because of the pressing costs for the vinyl and the need for distribution network.

Digital music reduces those costs and so albums become less important and singles more important.

Spotify, Apple Music et al, become arise because they become the way people find music.

In the process much of the old music industry died.
--
Using Shein, with all of it's flaws, as another example - the work heirarchy has been completely inverted. There aren't long meetings about reducing risk. There aren't seasonal cycles, they run small experiments, if an item takes off they do more, if it fails they look for another.experiment.

There are no silos and limited coordination overhead.

Ignoring the ethical and environmental implications of the way they do business, they're a very agile organization.

Shein's success isn't about doing individual tasks faster, but deliver the outcomes that the audience wants sooner.
--
## Ch 5 Rebundling the Job
Core claim - in a world where everyone has access to the same knowledge, there is knowledge overwhelm.

The promise of good taste and curation beats the promise of volume.

Leans into Theory of Constraints with a twist. Constraints are Scarcity, Risk and Coordination.

**Scarcity** - something that is a key resource is limited. In the case of shipping he shows that communications with the outside world - to keep up to date on schedule or summon help in emergency. So the radio operator with Morse code was the constraint. In modern software development the constraint is often Quality Assurance or Code Review.

**Risks** - Anaesthesiologist in a surgical environment. They're managing risk in the surgery. Paying attention to the patient's vital signs. Too much anaesthetic and the patients organs will shut down. Too little and they will wake up in the midst of the surgery.

**Coordination** - Many moving parts that need to align across groups. The book's example is getting a movie made. From writing, actors, sets, costumes, cinematography, funding, editing and ... . In this world the Producer is the coordinator and the becomes the constraint.

When all wine, good, bad and awful became more widely available the value of the sommelier increased. Wine is no longer scarce. Further, the internet is full of reviews about wine and vineyards. The constraint now is knowing where to look and who to trust. The sommelier is curating and instilling confidence. A restaurant uses them now as part of a package, promising people a better dining experience.

### Don't Chase the Skill, Follow the Constraint
Up skilling is still valuable, but only in the context of understanding the constraints first. Look to where the scarcity, risk or coordination constraints are and up skill for those problems.

> Skills are only valuable in relation to solving a constraint.

The evolution of the role of radiologists is a good example. They go from interpreting scans, to providing context for their colleagues. A shadow on a lung has a different meaning depending on the history of a patient. They participate more in the discussion of how to treat a cancer. *The implied claim that AI would get better than humans at reading X-ray and other images, still hasn't panned out.*

When constraints change, the roles that had value in the old case lose value. However, new roles emerge to tackle the new constraints.

The core claim of the book thus far: AI unbundles some tasks. Work that used to be valuable is no longer valuable. Instead of scarcity of skills, the constraints will be handling risk and coordination.

**Risks** with a new technology, we look for risks within the technology itself. Example elevators, the first question is what happens if the technology fails, will the elevator fall? The bigger risks come from the downstream effects. Elevators enable tall buildings, which have new structural and fire risks.

With GenAI one of the added layers of risk is the probabilistic nature of the systems.

**Coordination** tells a story of nurse navigators, helping patients deal with the increasingly messy journey through the hospital system. They use their expertise to coordinate. In the process they reduce the stress level for the patient and shorten the hospital stay.

The AI tools made some areas/departments work faster, but they were silos. The author calls this narrow. The nurse coordinator is working broadly across the whole system.

*We get to this better place, by helping people see the whole system and not the parts.*

==We only get rewarded when the value is made visible. It's not enough to improve the system if people don't see the value created.==

*Tidbit* - As AI execution scales, handling the exceptions (i.e. mislabel bins, damaged parts) becomes a much larger and more important job. The people who do this work in a warehouse do it informally and so are rarely noticed. It shows up in care environments, the system pays people for the task, yet the biggest value is the emotional support they provide.

Part of reimagining work will require making the invisible work (value?), visible to the system.

## Ch 6 Rebundling the Organization
Real Madrid, mid 2000s, built around star players. All given autonomy, yet they produced mediocre results. They optimized for individual play and didn't have a system. Barcelona, succeeded by having a system and giving players freedom within their zone.

The more complex the system, the more specialized the parts, the more important for there to be an explicit coordination system. Real Madrid failed because they lacked a system.

Mars Climate Orbiter is another example of coordination failure. One team did their math in pound-force and the other Newtons. Each team trusted the others competence and didn't question the numbers, they were experts after all. Small errors accumulated. The navigation system believed it was in the right place. When it tried to enter orbit, it instead hit the thin atmosphere and burned up. The teams had worked in isolation.

### Reducing the Coordination Tax with AI
The author claims that AI eliminates the tax. I'm troubled because he's ignoring the possibility of hallucination and the biases that the AI will add in.

He cites NotebookLLM, good. But also Persona generation. Not so good.

Leaning very heavily into Agentic execution to scout out and book sales calls -> agents to select suppliers.

Another good example is that burden of expense reporting has gone away. An AI pulls receipts from inboxes, categorizes and then sends them to the right people for approval. *Neither the employee, nor finance are dealing with the mess of expenses. A coordination tax has been eliminated*

The AI helps us when it aids the teams/organization to manage its own coordination. It enslaves us when it tells us what to do.

When we use AI in a narrow context i.e. within a single team, the team might go faster but the coordination tax goes up. Because the team using the AI produces more stuff than the other teams can handle. *This is classic Scrum deployment problem. A scrum team might significantly outpace the rest of the organization.*

> AI tool providers increasingly sell us: That AI will revolutionize knowledge work the way industrial automation revolutionized manufacturing. But there is a problem: knowledge work isn't like factory work.

Helping different teams coordinate their work, handle dependencies, work at different speeds and for different goals. This is where we need help.

Speed is not progress; Automation is not transformation.

## Ch 7. Rebundling the Value Chain

### Building Blocks on rent
The author makes the pitch that we more and more of what we need to build a business can be rented, as a series of building of blocks.

*Not super impressed with this section, where uses Mr Beast's Burger fiasco as a good and bad example*

Renting building blocks is ok to a point, what happens to quality? In addition, I can't see how this relates to AI.

# Section 3 Competitive Advantage 
## Ch 8 The Tool Integration Trap

  "id": "C28A66D8-A047-4FEB-9B75-7B0E43F22DC3",
  "title": "At #OPMMA #ProductCamp, I ran a session on GenAI and the future of Product Management. We ended up on code quality.",
  "content": "At #OPMMA #ProductCamp, I ran a session on GenAI and the future of Product Management. We ended up on code quality.\n\nSomeone in the audience said: \"My friend at a startup told me that they use GenAI to write all their code and it's great quality.\", They also said, \"Studies from last fall? They're outdated.\"\n\nI froze in the moment and missed the chance for a better response:\n- Risk profile for a startup is very different from a successful company\n- Code quality might be good for the first 100-200k lines of code, but that's not the long-term\n- The flaws that the studies find are about how the models are trained and rewarded. These are fundamental flaws; without changes to the process, the flaws will remain.\n- Anthropic says that Claude Code is generated code? Great! Look at the code from the March 31 leak. print.ts has a single function over 3000 lines and 12 levels of nesting. How do you test that?\n\nSee: https://agilepainrelief.com/blog/genai-code-quality-fundamental-flaws-and-how-bluffing-makes-it-worse/\n\nIn the medium term, I think we can do well with GenAI and code quality. The path likely leads through the existing Agile Engineering practices. Work in small increments, write rules and examples first. Use these as the specs for the code. Ensure the model only wrote code to satisfy the examples.\n\nWhy is my \"friend said\" so much more compelling than the evidence?\n",

  "content": "1. We will only import the subscribers, no point in importing un-subscribers. We can't email addresses we don't have.

4. One list vs multiple lists? Is there a benefit to having multiple lists?
5. Firstname and lastname custom attributes? Yes
6. Drip marker - yes
7. Cakemail tags must be simple. Let's use CamelCase.
8. We need to trim the list of tags - please suggest a starting point.
9. I can't imagine needing more than 5-10 tags per person at most: course(s) taken; how and where they signed up for the mailing list. Others ??
10. Cutover - hard switch when ready
11. All existing subscribers were double optin and so can be imported with the flag set to false.
12. Drip account shut down - no specific date, however there is no rollback. Once we cut over for newsletters, we're not going back. I will just keep the account open for a month in case we find a detail we missed.

content.text:
{
  "id": "A3B1AF22-0343-48D5-BA1A-FFFC1F3B1EA9",
  "title": "There are several clusters of interrelated problems that came up through our training. With apologies, this note will be mostly bullet points and a bit direct.",
  "content": "There are several clusters of interrelated problems that came up through our training. With apologies, this note will be mostly bullet points and a bit direct. 

## Product Ownership/Management
- Well-intentioned business stakeholders are attending backlog refinement and are helping to make detailed-level decisions. See: https://agilepainrelief.com/blog/jenga-effect-why-clients-dont-make-good-product-owners/ 
- Not enough resources and/or capacity to do all the work
- Challenges with Forecasting

Although it might not seem like it, all of these are related. No organization ever has enough capacity to do all the work. Even if we used my fairy dust and doubled the throughput of your teams, there still wouldn't be enough capacity.

Work on Forecasting:
- https://www.infoq.com/articles/sizing-forecasting-scrum/
- https://getnave.com/blog/estimation-in-kanban/
- https://agilepainrelief.com/blog/red-yellow-green-or-rygrag-reports-how-they-hide-the-truth/
With improved forecasting, we can engage the business in more realistic prioritization and tradeoff discussions.

Vision, Strategy and Saying NO.
- https://agilepainrelief.com/glossary/vision/ - a glossary entry that should have been a blog post
- https://agilepainrelief.com/blog/drowning-in-oversized-product-backlog-story-mapping-is-your-life-raft/ using a Story Map to help the PO and Team maintain focus
- https://agilepainrelief.com/blog/product-owners-and-the-art-of-saying-no/ 

Engage the business stakeholders at the appropriate level:
- https://agilepainrelief.com/blog/portfolio-management/
As I hinted at the start of this section, business people are not generally good product owners, because they don't have a good understanding of product development etc. We want their engagement, but at a level were they're helping to make big picture decisions i.e. we can choose among a few big items, which one to prioritize next.

## Teams
Departments of 8 and 12 are too big to be a single team (Scrum or otherwise): https://agilepainrelief.com/blog/scrum-team-size/ 

Groups of this size will be challenged to find a common goal (aka Vision). They also exhibit the problem that one person noted, "I'm rushing into a burning building, and I get no support because others don't see the urgency." This happens when we don't have a clear focus, Vision and Strategy (yet again I know).

Consider running an experiment, in both departments, forming true teams likely with 4 people. If possible, run the experiment as a self-selecting team activity (https://agilepainrelief.com/glossary/self-selecting-teams/), as it won't force change on anyone.

Run a team launch event: https://agilepainrelief.com/blog/how-to-build-a-powerful-team-from-scratch/ to help them kick off. 

(Making this work is going to require the Product Ownership work outlined above.)

## Real Bottleneck and Experimentation
These aren't related, I just wanted to make sure they're covered.

In the workshop, I outline the idea of a bigger picture Kanban board to improve overall flow and downstream bottlenecks:
https://agilepainrelief.com/blog/portfolio-management-with-upstream-and-downstream-teams/ 
https://www.amazon.ca/Flight-Levels-Leading-Organizations-Business-ebook/dp/B0CW1K1C7N/

// Experimental models that fit well with Scrum Teams
https://agilepainrelief.com/glossary/lean-startup/
https://agilepainrelief.com/glossary/lean-startup-experiments/
https://agilepainrelief.com/glossary/lean-ux/",

This wasn't on my list of quarterly goals, and so it has soaked up a …",
  "content": "

I've disappeared for the past two weeks; I needed to deal with some back-end issues. In particular, any of you who have been users of the Three Percent Better community have alread received a notification that it is shutting down. This wasn't on my list of quarterly goals, and so it has soaked up a considerable amount of my time. Later in 2026, I will consider launching a new discussion platform with a narrower focus. In the meantime, I apologize for any inconvenience the shutdown causes.

## AI Tsunami
I can't go even a few minutes without hearing more noise about AI. I've survived every Gartner Hype Cycle since they were established, and this is noisest of them all. Between 1995 and 2001, the dot-com bubble was based on the promise that the internet would change everything. It did, just a lot later than Nortel, JDS Uniphase, Pets.com and WebVan expected it to pay off.

AI is a louder, noisier version of the dot-com bubble. Real changes are happening, and they will impact our world. We can't predict whether this is a bubble or the beginning of a new era. If it's a bubble, we will still end up with GenAI tools with capabilities similar to those we have today. If it’s not a bubble and companies like OpenAI and Anthropic succeed, then the size of the changes will be much larger.

No matter what happens, we need to adapt to the changes, the only question is are these tools that augment our work or are corporations going to shrink?

Even if the tools don’t get better, they're already impacting our world. In software development, we already see more lines of code being written and more bugs being introduced: https://agilepainrelief.com/blog/ai-generated-code-quality-problems/. Yet, I also find teams that claim to be using AI and knocking it out of the park. Better quality than ever before.

As it currently stands, AI appears to be an amplifier. If you’re already doing well, AI seems to be a force multiplier. If you’re team/organization has challenges, AI will make them worse. Classic example: A team with either a bottleneck in either Decision-Making or Quality Assurance. They use AI to generate code, and now the bottleneck is worse. There are more decisions to make and larger product surface area to test.

## Agile More Relevant Than Ever
Agile has always been about adapting to change. GenAI requires us to: look for the bottlenecks; run more processes experiments and run more product experiments. From a product management perspective, I can already see that these tools make it easier to run more product experiments. My own experience, they make it easier to move my data from one product to another. Without good Quality and Product Market Fit, speed doesn’t matter.

There is a lot of work ahead of us, to explore this new territory.

Pssst, I still write about Scrum: [Product Backlog Refinement Hell: 3 Problems and Solutions](https://agilepainrelief.com/blog/product-backlog-refinement-hell-solutions/)

## Help Me Name What I'm doing
What I want to be is the person you trust to share both sides the good and the bad. Someone mapping the territory as it actually is, not as vendors promise it will be.

I've been searching for a label that captures that middle ground. Three candidates:

🗺️ AI Cartographer - mapping the terrain, cliffs and all 
🏔️ AI Sherpa - trusted guide through difficult, uncertain territory 
📐 AI Surveyor - measuring what is really on the ground

Which one resonates with you? Tell me why you voted. Or suggest something better.

## What’s Next?
I'm off for the next two and a half weeks, exploring the Canary Islands (warmer than Ottawa in March) and trying to understand my place in this fast changing world.


",
